title: They like you more than you think
rule: After a chat, people tend to like you more than you guess.

examples.work:
Rahul: "Good luck with the demo!"
You (thinking): "I talked too much about that bug."
Rahul (later, to Priya): "He's really easy to talk to."
examples.everyday:
You: "Sorry, I went on and on about my cricket team."
Riya: "Are you kidding? That was the best part of the evening."

insteadOf: That was awkward. She must think I'm boring.
analogy: You cringe at your voice on a recording. Everyone else just hears you.
tryPrompt: Name one person you chatted with this week. Say one thing they probably enjoyed about that chat.

title: People care what you share
rule: People care more about what you share than you expect.

examples.work:
Fatima: "What did you do on Sunday?"
You: "Tried baking bread for the first time. It came out like a brick! Do you bake?"
Fatima: "Ha! Yes, send me a photo!"
examples.everyday:
Cousin: "What's new with you?"
You: "I've started cycling to work on Fridays. My legs are not happy! Do you still go running?"

insteadOf: Nobody wants to hear about my weekend.
analogy: Like cooking for friends: you worry it's plain, then they ask for seconds.
tryPrompt: Pick one small thing from your weekend you'd normally skip. Say it in two sentences, then ask a question.

title: Most people want to talk too
rule: People nearby are often happy to chat; someone just has to start.

examples.work:
You (in the lift): "Long day, or just getting started?"
Joseph: "Just starting! Three calls before lunch."
You: "Three before lunch? Which one's the big one?"
examples.everyday:
You (at the bus stop): "Is the 500D running late again?"
Aunty: "Always! Twenty minutes, at least. Where are you headed?"

insteadOf: Don't disturb him. He probably wants some quiet.
analogy: At a bus stop, everyone waits for someone else to speak first. Go first.
tryPrompt: Say one easy line you could use in the lift or at the coffee machine tomorrow.

title: A tiny chat lifts your day
rule: A few friendly words with a stranger can lift your mood.

examples.work:
You (at the front desk): "Morning! Did the rain flood the car park again?"
Guard: "Only the back row. Park near the gate today."
You: "Thanks, will do. Has it been raining since last night?"
examples.everyday:
You (at the chai stall): "Ginger chai today? It smells amazing."
Chai seller: "Fresh ginger, just came in. One or two?"

insteadOf: Grabbing your chai without a word or a look.
analogy: A smile at the chai stall is like a pinch of sugar: tiny, but you taste it.
tryPrompt: Tomorrow, say one friendly line to a shopkeeper, guard or driver. Practise the line aloud now.

title: "Fine" closes the door
rule: A one-word answer gives them nothing to say back.

examples.work:
Arjun: "How was your day?"
You: "Long, but we fixed the login bug at last. How was yours?"
Arjun: "Wait, the one from Monday? Finally!"
examples.everyday:
Mom (on the phone): "How's everything?"
You: "All good! I tried making your rajma. What's your secret?"

insteadOf: "How was your day?" — "Fine."
analogy: A one-word answer is a dot ball: nothing happens, nobody runs.
tryPrompt: Answer "How was your day?" once with one word, then once with something real. Hear the difference.

title: Feeling first, then one fact
rule: Start with how it felt, then add one real thing that happened.

examples.work:
Rahul: "How was the offsite?"
You: "Fun, actually! We did a cooking challenge and our team won. Were you at the Pune one?"
Rahul: "Yes, we just did quizzes. Jealous!"
examples.everyday:
Friend: "How was the wedding?"
You: "Exhausting but lovely. The dhol played till 2 a.m. Have you been to one that went that late?"

insteadOf: "How was the offsite?" — "Nice."
analogy: The feeling is the headline. The detail is the photo under it.
tryPrompt: How was yesterday? Say one feeling word first, like a headline, then one real thing.
credit: The Reveal step in Carol Fleming's ARE

title: Names beat "nice"
rule: Names, places and food give them more than "nice" or "good".

examples.work:
Priya: "What did you do last night?"
You: "Watched the India match at Arjun's place. Did you catch the last over?"
examples.everyday:
Neighbour: "Good dinner?"
You: "Great. Pav bhaji from the cart near the station. Have you tried it?"

insteadOf: "What did you do last night?" — "Something nice."
analogy: "Nice food" is a blurry photo. "Pav bhaji near the station" is in focus.
tryPrompt: Describe last weekend in two sentences. Use one name, one place and one food. No "nice".

title: Leave a thread to pull
rule: Drop a small detail they can ask about. That's a thread.

examples.work:
Joseph: "How was your weekend?"
You: "Good! I went on a trek and got caught in the rain. You?"
Joseph: "Wait, which trek? I want to try one."
examples.everyday:
Aunty: "What's new?"
You: "I've started learning the guitar. Three chords so far! Do you still sing?"
Aunty: "Three chords is enough for an old Kishore Kumar song!"

insteadOf: "How was your weekend?" — "Good. Relaxed."
analogy: A loose thread on your sleeve: people can't help pulling it.
tryPrompt: Answer "How was your weekend?" with one detail someone would want to ask about.

title: Keep a fresh detail ready
rule: Each morning, pick one thing from yesterday to share if asked.

examples.work:
Fatima: "Anything new?"
You: "I found a back road that cuts ten minutes off my commute. Which way do you come in?"
examples.everyday:
Brother (on a call): "So, what's up?"
You: "I watched a show on Lucknow street food. Now I'm planning a trip! Want to come?"

insteadOf: "Anything new?" — "Nothing, same old."
analogy: Like keeping change ready for the auto: when the moment comes, you're not searching.
tryPrompt: Pick your fresh detail from yesterday right now. Say it in one sentence, then add a question.

title: Two sentences, not a speech
rule: Keep your answer to two sentences, three at most, then hand over.

examples.work:
Riya: "How was Goa?"
You: "Brilliant. The best part was a beach shack playing old Hindi songs. Have you been?"
examples.everyday:
Uncle: "How's the new job?"
You: "Really good so far. My team takes chai breaks very seriously! How's retired life?"

insteadOf: A five-minute, day-by-day tour of your whole Goa trip.
analogy: A good answer is a T20 over, not a Test match.
tryPrompt: Answer "How's work these days?" in two sentences: the point first, one detail, then a question.

title: End with a hook
rule: Finish your answer with a question, so the turn passes to them.

examples.work:
Rahul: "How was your day?"
You: "Busy. The audit took all morning. How's your week going?"
Rahul: "Don't ask! Two deadlines on Friday."
examples.everyday:
Friend: "How was the movie?"
You: "So good. The ending really surprised me. Have you seen it?"

insteadOf: "How was your day?" — "Busy. We had the audit." (silence)
analogy: Conversation is badminton, not a speech. Hit the shuttle back to their side.
tryPrompt: Answer "How was your morning?" and end with a question back.

title: A sharper hook than "You?"
rule: A specific question back is easier to answer than "And you?"

examples.work:
Priya: "How's the sprint?"
You: "Tight, but we'll meet the deadline. Is your team stuck on testing too?"
examples.everyday:
Cousin: "How was your day?"
You: "Busy, but good. I fixed a bug I'd been stuck on all week. Calm day for you, or a crazy one?"

insteadOf: "…And you?"
analogy: "And you?" is a loose throw. A specific question lands right in their hands.
tryPrompt: Answer "How's your week?" Then end with a specific question, not "And you?"

title: Take turns sharing
rule: Share a little, then let them share. Taking turns tends to build liking.

examples.work:
Fatima: "Weekend plans?"
You: "Just a long cycle ride on Sunday morning. What about you?"
Fatima: "My sister's visiting. We might do Lalbagh."
You: "Lalbagh's lovely now. Is the flower show on?"
examples.everyday:
Neighbour: "We went to Mysore on Sunday."
You: "Lovely! We just stayed home and made dosas. Did you see the palace?"

insteadOf: Telling your whole story while they only nod.
analogy: Like a plate of pakoras: you take one, then pass the plate.
tryPrompt: A colleague says, "I went to my hometown last weekend." Share one line about yours, then ask them something.

title: Yes or no? Add a bit more
rule: Answer a yes-or-no question with the answer, one detail and a question.

examples.work:
Arjun: "Did you watch the match?"
You: "Missed it, sadly! I was stuck on a call. Was it a good one?"
Arjun: "Last-ball finish!"
examples.everyday:
Shopkeeper: "Tried the new mango barfi?"
You: "Not yet! Is it better than the kaju one? I'll take a small box."

insteadOf: "Did you watch the match?" — "No."
analogy: "No" is a red light. "No, but…" turns it green.
tryPrompt: Someone asks, "Have you tried the new canteen menu?" Answer yes or no, add one detail, then a question.

title: Turn it into an invitation
rule: Sometimes the best hook is an offer: "Want to grab one?"

examples.work:
Priya: "Long day?"
You: "Long, but okay. I really need chai. Want to grab one?"
Priya: "Yes, please. Ten minutes?"
examples.everyday:
Friend: "I'm so bored this weekend."
You: "Same! There's a food festival near the lake on Sunday. Want to go?"

insteadOf: "Long day?" — "Hmm."
analogy: An offer is like holding the lift door: a small gesture that says "come along".
tryPrompt: A colleague says, "So much work today." Reply with one detail and an offer.

title: Bad day? Say it lightly
rule: If your day went badly, say so, with a small smile in it.

examples.work:
Rahul: "How's it going?"
You: "Rough one. My laptop crashed twice before lunch. Yours better?"
Rahul: "Ha, a bit. Want me to call IT?"
examples.everyday:
Mom: "How was the trip back?"
You: "Long! The train was four hours late, but I finished a whole book. What did you all have for dinner?"

insteadOf: "How was your day?" — "Terrible. Everything went wrong."
analogy: Like rain at a picnic: you mention it, laugh, and still pass the sandwiches.
tryPrompt: Think of one small thing that went wrong this week. Say it lightly in one line, then ask back.

title: Corridor "How are you?"
rule: In a corridor, "How are you?" is a hello. Reply in one line.

examples.work:
Joseph (walking past): "Hey, how are you?"
You: "Good, thanks! Surviving Monday. You?"
Joseph: "Same! Catch you later."
examples.everyday:
Neighbour (in the lift): "All well?"
You: "All good! Off to the market. You?"

insteadOf: A full update on your week, or silence.
analogy: A wave from a passing car. You wave back; you don't chase the car.
tryPrompt: Practise three one-line replies to a quick "How are you?" in the corridor. Keep each under eight words.
credit: Debra Fine, The Fine Art of Small Talk

title: A small slip beats silence
rule: A tiny grammar slip matters less than an answer that stops the chat.

examples.work:
Priya: "How was the client visit?"
You: "Went well! They really liked the new dashboard. Were you on the call?"
examples.everyday:
Friend: "How's Bengaluru treating you?"
You: "The traffic's crazy, but the weather's lovely. When are you visiting?"

insteadOf: Staying quiet because you're unsure of the grammar.
analogy: A fielder who fumbles keeps playing. Standing frozen gives away more runs.
tryPrompt: Answer "How was your morning?" right now, without stopping to fix anything. Keep going for two sentences.

title: Share a small win
rule: A small win from today is an easy, happy answer.

examples.work:
Arjun: "How was the meeting?"
You: "Better than I expected. They actually liked the new design! How was yours?"
examples.everyday:
Friend: "What's new?"
You: "I cooked dinner without burning anything, finally! Want to come over on Sunday and try it?"

insteadOf: "How was the meeting?" — "Fine."
analogy: Like a single off the last ball: small, but everyone cheers.
tryPrompt: Name one small win from this week. Say it as an answer to "What's new?", then ask back.

title: Sound like you talk
rule: Short, spoken sentences sound warmer than formal ones.

examples.work:
Fatima: "How are you doing?"
You: "I'm good! A bit sleepy. The team dinner ran late. You?"
examples.everyday:
Cousin: "How's life?"
You: "Pretty good. I've started a little balcony garden. Do you still grow chillies?"

insteadOf: "I am doing well, thank you for asking."
analogy: Formal English over chai is like wearing a suit to the beach.
tryPrompt: Answer "How are you doing?" starting with "I'm", plus one short detail. Short words only.

title: "Where are you from?"
rule: Give the place plus one thing about it, then ask theirs.

examples.work:
Joseph: "Where are you from?"
You: "Indore originally, but I've been in Pune six years now. I still miss the poha there. You?"
examples.everyday:
Fellow passenger: "Going home?"
You: "Yes, to Nagpur. My mom's already planning the menu! Is Nagpur home for you too?"

insteadOf: "Where are you from?" — "Delhi."
analogy: Your hometown is a free story you carry everywhere. Open the bag a little.
tryPrompt: Answer "Where are you from?" with your town, one thing you miss and a question back.

title: "What do you do?"
rule: Say your job in plain words, plus what you actually do.

examples.work:
Riya (at a meetup): "What do you do?"
You: "I'm a product manager. I decide what our learning app builds next. What about you?"
examples.everyday:
Uncle: "So what exactly do you do?"
You: "I help build an app that teaches English. Lots of talking to users! Want to try it?"

insteadOf: "What do you do?" — "I'm a PM."
analogy: A job title is a closed lunchbox. Show them what's inside.
tryPrompt: Explain your job to a new neighbour in two plain sentences, then ask about theirs.

title: "Any plans for the weekend?"
rule: No plans? Say what you might do, then ask about theirs.

examples.work:
Priya: "Any plans for the long weekend?"
You: "Nothing big. I might finally try that trek near Lonavala. Are you going anywhere?"
examples.everyday:
Friend: "What are you up to this evening?"
You: "Probably cooking and a call with my parents. Something fun on your side?"

insteadOf: "Any plans for the weekend?" — "Not really."
analogy: Even a quiet weekend has a trailer. Show them one scene.
tryPrompt: A colleague asks, "Any plans for Sunday?" Answer with one maybe-plan and a question back.

title: "How was the festival?"
rule: Share one warm detail from the festival, then ask about their break.

examples.work:
Joseph: "How was Diwali?"
You: "Lovely. My mom's kaju katli is dangerous! How was your long weekend?"
examples.everyday:
Fatima: "Eid Mubarak! Did you get the biryani I sent?"
You: "Eid Mubarak! We finished it in ten minutes. What's the secret?"

insteadOf: "How was Diwali?" — "Good."
analogy: Festival talk is like sharing sweets: pass one piece, then hold the box out.
tryPrompt: A colleague asks, "How was your long weekend?" Answer with one festival or holiday detail, then ask about theirs.

title: "Busy day?"
rule: "Busy?" deserves more than "yes": say what's keeping you busy.

examples.work:
Rahul: "Busy day?"
You: "Very! Two launches at once. How's your week looking?"
Rahul: "Calmer, thankfully. Need a hand?"
examples.everyday:
Shop owner: "Busy these days?"
You: "Yes, my sister has board exams, so the whole house is on mute! Busy here too?"

insteadOf: "Busy day?" — "Yes."
analogy: "Yes" is a missed call. Say a full line and they'll call back.
tryPrompt: Someone asks, "Busy week?" Say what's keeping you busy in one line, then ask back.

title: Hear the extra detail
rule: Listen for the extra detail they drop: a place, a name, a plan.

examples.work:
Rahul: "Weekend was good. I was at my cousin's engagement in Jaipur."
You: "Jaipur! Was it a big function?"
Rahul: "Huge. Four hundred people!"
examples.everyday:
Friend: "Sorry I'm late, I was at the vet with Bruno."
You: "Oh no, is Bruno okay?"

insteadOf: Hearing only "good" and missing the rest.
analogy: Their answer is a menu. Spot the dish you'd like to hear more about.
tryPrompt: A colleague says, "Long weekend. I drove to Coorg with college friends." Name the two details you heard.

title: Ask about their thread
rule: Ask about what they just said, not a brand-new topic.

examples.work:
Fatima: "I went to Pune this weekend."
You: "Oh nice, what took you there?"
Fatima: "My best friend's housewarming."
examples.everyday:
Brother: "I've joined a badminton club."
You: "Since when? Are you any good?"

insteadOf: "I went to Pune." — "Nice. Did you watch the match?"
analogy: One deep well beats ten shallow holes.
tryPrompt: A colleague says, "I spent Sunday at a pottery class." Ask one question about it.

title: Short news, short question
rule: When they share a little, ask one short question about it.

examples.work:
Joseph: "I went hiking on Saturday."
You: "Oh, where? Was it tough?"
Joseph: "Skandagiri. The last stretch was brutal!"
examples.everyday:
Riya: "I finally got my licence."
You: "Finally! Two-wheeler or car?"

insteadOf: "I went hiking." — "Nice."
analogy: Like a gentle push on a swing: a small nudge keeps it going.
tryPrompt: Your friend texts, "Just got back from Ooty." Reply with one short question.

title: Pick the warmer thread
rule: Two details? Ask about the one they sound excited about.

examples.work:
Priya: "Crazy week. Two client calls, and I'm running my first 10K on Sunday!"
You: "Your first 10K! How long have you been training?"
examples.everyday:
Uncle: "Busy month. The house is being painted, and I've started yoga."
You: "Yoga! How's it going so far?"

insteadOf: Asking about the client calls when they're clearly excited about the race.
analogy: Two snacks on the plate? Reach for the one that's still warm.
tryPrompt: A friend says, "Work's busy, but I'm learning to make sourdough." Pick the warmer thread and ask about it.

title: Rescue with an earlier thread
rule: When the chat goes quiet, go back to something they said earlier.

examples.work:
(Silence by the coffee machine)
You: "Wait, you said you're running a 10K on Sunday. Nervous?"
Priya: "Very! I've never run that far."
examples.everyday:
(The chat slows down)
You: "Hey, you mentioned Jaipur earlier. Did you eat anything good?"
Rahul: "Dal baati, three times!"

insteadOf: Awkward silence, then "So… okay."
analogy: A dying fire? Blow on the coal that's still glowing.
tryPrompt: Remember something a colleague mentioned this week. Say the line you'd use to bring it back up.

title: Comment, question, comment
rule: Mix comments with questions, so it never feels like an interview.

examples.work:
Arjun: "I just moved to Whitefield."
You: "That's a big change from Jayanagar. How's the commute?"
Arjun: "Shorter, thankfully."
You: "Lucky you. Mine's an hour each way."
examples.everyday:
Friend: "We tried that new Korean place."
You: "I've walked past it so many times. Was it spicy?"

insteadOf: "Where did you go? Who with? How long? What did you eat?"
analogy: Only questions is a police interview. Add comments and it's a chat over chai.
tryPrompt: A colleague says, "I've started gardening." Reply with a comment, then a question.

title: Comment on what you both see
rule: Stuck? Comment on something you can both see right now.

examples.work:
(Silence in the lift)
You: "This lift is slower than our release cycle! Are you on eight too?"
Joseph: "Nine. Same pain."
examples.everyday:
(A quiet moment at the wedding)
You: "The dhol player hasn't stopped for an hour. Are you dancing later?"
Cousin: "Only if you do!"

insteadOf: Staring at your phone in a silent lift.
analogy: What you both see is free chutney at the counter: always there, help yourself.
tryPrompt: Think of where you'll be at lunch tomorrow. Say one comment about it, then one question.

title: "Speaking of…"
rule: Take one word they said and link it to your own small story.

examples.work:
Fatima: "We watched a movie with the whole team last night."
You: "Speaking of movies, I finally saw 12th Fail. Have you seen it?"
examples.everyday:
Friend: "My mom made appam this morning."
You: "Speaking of appam, there's a new Kerala café near my flat. Want to try it on Saturday?"

insteadOf: "Okay." (and the topic ends)
analogy: Like a train switching tracks at a junction: same journey, smooth turn.
tryPrompt: Someone says, "I spent the weekend reading." Use "Speaking of…" to link to something of yours, then ask.

title: Laugh along
rule: When they joke about something ordinary, laugh back. It shows you want to connect.

examples.work:
Rahul: "My code works and I have no idea why."
You: "Ha! Don't touch it. Is it going live today?"
examples.everyday:
Aunty: "I asked for less sugar. This is basically syrup!"
You: "Ha, classic! Shall I ask for another one?"

insteadOf: A straight face and "Okay."
analogy: A laugh back is a high five: they raise a hand, you meet it.
tryPrompt: A colleague jokes, "The Wi-Fi only works when the boss is here." Laugh, then add one line.

title: Let them talk about themselves
rule: People enjoy talking about their own lives, so give them room.

examples.work:
Joseph: "I've started baking on weekends."
You: "Nice! What do you bake?"
Joseph: "Banana bread, mostly. Now my kids expect it every Sunday."
examples.everyday:
Grandma: "In my day, we walked to school."
You: "How far was it? Tell me about it."

insteadOf: Turning every answer back to your own week.
analogy: Asking about their hobby is handing them the karaoke mic. Most secretly want it.
tryPrompt: Today, ask a friend one question about something they love. Then just listen for a minute.

title: Mirror one word
rule: A negotiation expert suggests repeating their key word as a question.

examples.work:
Priya: "The client changed the whole brief again."
You: "The whole brief?"
Priya: "Yes! Even the colours. We start from scratch on Monday."
examples.everyday:
Friend: "I'm thinking of quitting the gym."
You: "Quitting?"
Friend: "It's too far. I want one closer to home."

insteadOf: "Oh." (and you change the topic)
analogy: Like a waiter reading your order back: you feel heard straight away.
tryPrompt: A colleague says, "The demo crashed in front of the whole team." Mirror one word aloud.

title: Wait two seconds
rule: After they finish, wait two seconds. They often say more.

examples.work:
Arjun: "The review went okay."
You: (wait… two seconds)
Arjun: "Actually, they want me to lead the next one."
You: "That's big! What will it involve?"
examples.everyday:
Mom: "Your dad tried cooking today."
You: (wait…)
Mom: "He made upma. It was… crunchy."

insteadOf: Jumping in the moment they stop.
analogy: Waiting two seconds is like letting tea brew: more flavour comes out.
tryPrompt: Ask someone about their day tonight. When they stop, count two seconds before you speak.

title: Echo once, not every line
rule: Mirror once or twice in a chat. More than that sounds fake.

examples.work:
Rahul: "Mad week with the audit."
You: "The audit?"
Rahul: "Yes, and the deadline moved up."
You: "Ouch. When is it now?"
examples.everyday:
Friend: "I'm moving to Hyderabad."
You: "Hyderabad?"
Friend: "New job! Next month."
You: "Congratulations! Which part of the city?"

insteadOf: "The audit?" … "The deadline?" … "The weekend?"
analogy: Salt once makes the dal. Salt every minute ruins it.
tryPrompt: Start from "I've joined a dance class." Mirror once, then ask a normal question.
credit: Leil Lowndes (parroting); a critic's warning, via book summaries

title: React before you ask
rule: Show a small reaction first, like "Japan!", then ask your question.

examples.work:
Fatima: "I just got back from Japan."
You: "Japan! What surprised you the most?"
Fatima: "How quiet the trains were!"
examples.everyday:
Cousin: "I cleared my driving test."
You: "No way, first try? When's the road trip?"

insteadOf: "I just got back from Japan." — "Okay. What did you see?"
analogy: A reaction is the clap before the speech. It tells them you're with them.
tryPrompt: Your friend says, "I just ran my first half marathon." React in one or two words, then ask one question.

title: Go where the chat goes
rule: If the talk turns somewhere surprising, follow it instead of pulling it back.

examples.work:
Joseph: "So the report's late. Oh, and I'm learning the tabla now."
You: "Tabla! How's that going?"
Joseph: "Three months in! My neighbour teaches me."
examples.everyday:
Friend: "Traffic was bad. Oh, and I saw an elephant on the highway!"
You: "An elephant? Where was it going?"

insteadOf: "Anyway, about the report…"
analogy: Like an auto driver's shortcut: trust the turn, you might enjoy the route.
tryPrompt: A colleague says mid-update, "By the way, I adopted a cat." Say what you'd reply.

title: Tired? Reply calmly
rule: When someone sounds tired, match them with a calm, gentle reply.

examples.work:
Priya: "Ugh, what a week."
You: "Tell me about it. Chai first, then emails?"
Priya: "Yes. Please."
examples.everyday:
Brother: "Just got home. So tired."
You: "Long day? Eat something and rest. We'll talk tomorrow."

insteadOf: A loud, cheerful "Come on, cheer up!"
analogy: If they're dancing to a slow song, don't start doing bhangra.
tryPrompt: A colleague sighs, "Third late night this week." Reply in a calm, tired tone. Keep it short.

title: Excited? Get excited too
rule: When they're excited, show some excitement back before you ask.

examples.work:
Rahul: "We won the hackathon!"
You: "No way! That's huge! What did you build?"
examples.everyday:
Riya: "I got tickets for the final!"
You: "You did? Lucky you! Who are you going with?"

insteadOf: "We won the hackathon!" — "Okay, congrats."
analogy: Like a Mexican wave in the stadium: when they stand up, you stand up too.
tryPrompt: A friend texts, "My startup got its first paying customer!" Reply with their energy, then one question.

title: Don't argue with their mood
rule: Agree with how they feel first. Don't flip it.

examples.work:
Arjun: "Ugh, Mondays."
You: "I know. My inbox doubled overnight. Coffee?"
examples.everyday:
Friend: "This heat is unbearable."
You: "It really is. I've had three nimbu panis already. Want one?"

insteadOf: "Ugh, Mondays." — "Actually, I love Mondays!"
analogy: Raining outside? Don't tell them it's sunny. Hand them an umbrella.
tryPrompt: Someone says, "This traffic is the worst." Agree first, add one detail, then ask something.

title: Bad news? Slow down
rule: When they share bad news, drop the jokes and ask gently.

examples.work:
Fatima: "The client rejected the whole deck."
You: "Oh no, after all that work. What did they say?"
examples.everyday:
Friend: "My flight got cancelled. I'll miss my sister's wedding."
You: "Oh no, that's awful. Is there another way to get there?"

insteadOf: "Ha, classic client! Anyway…"
analogy: Like driving past a school: slow down, look carefully, no honking.
tryPrompt: A colleague says, "My laptop died and I lost a week of work." Reply gently in two sentences.

title: Practical question? Help first
rule: If they need something practical, answer it first. Chat later.

examples.work:
Joseph: "Do you know where the projector remote is?"
You: "Top drawer in room four. Big presentation today?"
examples.everyday:
Neighbour: "Which bus goes to the station?"
You: "The blue one, from that stop. It comes every ten minutes. Off to work?"

insteadOf: "Where's the projector remote?" — a story about your first week.
analogy: Like a headline: the answer goes first, the chat comes after.
tryPrompt: A new colleague asks, "Where's the canteen?" Answer first in one line, then add one friendly question.

title: Don't top their story
rule: When they share something, don't jump in with a bigger story of yours.

examples.work:
Arjun: "I ran my first 5K on Sunday!"
You: "Your first! How did it feel at the finish?"
Arjun: "Like I could do it again. Almost."
examples.everyday:
Cousin: "We got stuck in a two-hour traffic jam."
You: "Two hours! What did you do the whole time?"

insteadOf: "You ran 5K? I ran a half marathon last year."
analogy: It's their innings. Don't walk out to bat while they're still batting.
tryPrompt: A friend says, "I finally visited Kashmir!" Reply without mentioning your own trip. Ask one question.
credit: Celeste Headlee (TED talk, via a third-party summary)

title: Skip "I know exactly how you feel"
rule: Don't claim you know exactly how they feel. Ask about their experience.

examples.work:
Priya: "The first week in a new team is hard."
You: "I can imagine. What's been the hardest part so far?"
examples.everyday:
Friend: "Moving cities is exhausting."
You: "That's a lot to handle. How's the new place so far?"

insteadOf: "I know exactly how you feel. When I moved…"
analogy: Everyone's shoes pinch in a different spot. Ask where theirs pinch.
tryPrompt: A colleague says, "My first presentation went badly." Reply with one kind line and one question about it.
credit: Celeste Headlee (TED talk, via a third-party summary)

title: "Me too" closes it
rule: Instead of only "me too", ask about their side.

examples.work:
Rahul: "I'm so tired."
You: "Late night? Or just one of those weeks?"
Rahul: "Late night. The release went out at 2 a.m."
examples.everyday:
Friend: "I love this song."
You: "Same! When did you first hear it?"

insteadOf: "I'm so tired." — "Me too."
analogy: "Me too" is a full stop. A question is a comma.
tryPrompt: A colleague says, "I'm so hungry." Reply with a question instead of just "me too".

title: Your story can wait
rule: Ask one more question about theirs before you share your own.

examples.work:
Fatima: "I spent the weekend in Goa."
You: "Goa! Which beach were you near?"
Fatima: "Palolem. So quiet."
You: "I loved Palolem too. Did you try kayaking?"
examples.everyday:
Friend: "My grandma taught me her pickle recipe."
You: "Lucky you! Which pickle?"
Friend: "Mango. It took two days!"

insteadOf: "Oh, Goa! When I went to Goa…"
analogy: Let their chai finish before you pour yours.
tryPrompt: A friend says, "We drove to Pondicherry." You've been too. Ask one question before you mention your trip.

title: Share smaller, then hand back
rule: If you share your own story, keep it smaller and end with a question.

examples.work:
Joseph: "Our flight was delayed six hours."
You: "Six! Mine was delayed two hours once, and that felt endless. How did you pass the time?"
examples.everyday:
Riya: "My cat knocked my phone into the sink."
You: "Oh no! Mine once sat on my laptop mid-call. Is the phone okay?"

insteadOf: A ten-minute story about your own worst flight.
analogy: Add one small brick to their wall. Don't build your own house.
tryPrompt: A colleague says, "My train broke down for an hour." Share one smaller line of yours, then ask a question.
